Welcome to the National Natural History Museum. This audio guide will introduce you to our main galleries and help you make the most of your visit. Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable phenomena in the natural world, bird migration. Each year, roughly half of all bird species on Earth undertake some form of seasonal movement, some travelling only a few hundred kilometres, others crossing entire hemispheres. But how do they do it, and why? To place the bird migration lecture in perspective, we need to distinguish the familiar modern description from the longer process that produced it. Within the bird migration lecture, what now appears stable often emerged through small changes whose significance became visible only later. A simple list of events in the bird migration lecture can hide those alternatives, so the discussion will emphasise why particular changes mattered. Let's start with the why. Migration is fundamentally a response to seasonal changes in food availability. During summer in the northern hemisphere, insects, seeds and fruits are abundant, and the long daylight hours allow birds to forage for long periods. In winter approaches, food becomes scarce. Rather than staying and struggling, migrating birds travel to regions where conditions are more favourable. Evidence for the bird migration lecture does not come from a single source. Researchers may compare controlled findings with patterns observed outside the laboratory. Each source answers a different question and carries its own uncertainty. Agreement can increase confidence, while disagreement often reveals an assumption or a measurement problem that deserves closer examination. Now the how is even more fascinating. Birds use multiple navigational systems simultaneously. First and most importantly, many species navigate using Earth's magnetic field. Researchers have discovered that birds have magnetite crystals in their beaks, effectively biological compasses. A 2019 study confirmed that disrupting magnetic fields can disorient migrating birds even in clear conditions. Second, birds use the position of the sun during the day and the stars at night. Young birds seem to have an innate star map. They learn the night sky during their first summer, before they have ever migrated and use this knowledge later. Scale is especially important when evaluating the bird migration lecture. A process observed in one case, one community or one short trial, may behave differently across a region or over several generations. In this bird migration lecture, examples at different scales will therefore be compared. This comparison helps identify which conditions are essential and which are merely helpful. Third, birds rely on familiar landscape features. Coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges, and visual landmarks, particularly during the final stages of a journey. It is also worth noticing the language of certainty used in the bird migration lecture. Some mechanisms are supported by direct observation, while others remain the best explanation available from indirect evidence. The final account should separate established patterns from reasonable inference. Keep that distinction in mind as the examples are brought together. Interestingly, many small songbirds migrate at night, when there is less wind turbulence and fewer predators. Larger birds like geese and swans travel during the day, often in V formations which reduce wind resistance and conserve energy. This is also a good example of a migration. Many species are shifting their migration timing, arriving earlier in spring as temperatures rise. This sounds positive, but it can cause a mismatch. Birds may arrive before their food sources, the insects they feed on, have become available. This is called a phenological mismatch, and it is emerging as one of the key threats to migratory bird populations worldwide. The separate examples in the bird migration lecture can finally be organised around three questions. What conditions begin to change, which mechanisms sustain it, and what consequences appear later? For the bird migration lecture, that structure keeps chronology from becoming a list of disconnected facts. The conclusion to the bird migration lecture will use that framework to connect the details without extending them beyond the available evidence. Conservation efforts are focusing on protecting key stopover sites, the staging areas where birds rest and refuel mid-journey. Losing even one critical stopover site can have devastating effects on an entire species population. A useful final check is to ask what observation would make the present account of the bird migration lecture less convincing. Identifying such evidence keeps the explanation testable and reveals where future research would be most informative. It also prevents a plausible narrative from being treated as complete merely because its separate examples fit together. Thank you. We'll now move on to look at specific case studies.
